verses.1: Al-Mizan takes the earth’s possessive zilzālahā to mark a particular quake of utmost terror, intensity, and magnitude.
verses.2: Al-Mizan notes that athqāl can mean provisions or commodities, or loads and burdens. Here it has been read as the dead, buried treasures and precious metals, or both; it prefers the dead, then the inclusive reading. The earth thus sends forth the dead from their graves for ḥisāb, reckoning, and then jazāʾ, recompense.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says people, stupefied by the terrible earthquake, ask what is wrong with the earth and why it shakes. It records the view that al-insān means only deniers of the afterlife, rather than believers, while noting other views follow.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says the earth will testify to the children of Adam’s deeds alongside their limbs, angelic scribes, and other human and non-human witnesses. Because God inspires it, the earth consciously retains the good and evil committed on it and will disclose its record when commanded. The commentary infers from this, and from related verses, that life and consciousness pervade all things although people may not perceive them. It therefore finds no need for alternatives that make the earth newly alive, give it a created voice, or reduce its testimony to lisān al-ḥāl; those alternatives also do not make it a decisive judicial witness.

verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that people issue forth in varied groups from the place of accounting toward paradise or hell, the happy distinguished from the wretched. Being shown their deeds may mean seeing their recompense in their final abodes or seeing the deeds themselves under tajassum al-aʿmāl, the embodiment of deeds; it finds the first more apparent. It also records the view that they emerge from graves already differing in face, peace, and terror, and that ‘showing’ means informing them of recompense through reckoning, but again judges the first reading clearer.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes the two verses as the consequence of being shown one’s deeds: no good or evil, even an atom’s weight, escapes being seen by its doer, and the separate statements establish a universal law for both classes. This does not contradict more specific rulings in which deeds vanish, pass between people—for example between killer and victim—or evil deeds are changed to good through repentance. Those rulings qualify the general law: one who has lost good deeds has none to be shown.
